passage: I'm Kalyani, Arnab's older sister. On Sunday he spent a whole hour on the long-division sums Baba set for him, rubbing out, starting again, muttering. He did finish them. But afterwards he was like a different boy. He went straight to the kitchen and ate three of the biscuits Ma had saved for guests, even though he knows the rule. When I said, "Those were for Mashi," he shouted, "You always tattle!" and slammed the door. He's usually the patient one. Ma said, "His brain is tired, let him be." I'm not sure that's the whole reason. Maybe he was also just fed up with sums. After an hour of cricket outside, he came back and said sorry about the biscuits.

qa.q: How many of the guests' biscuits did Arnab eat?
qa.a: He ate three of the biscuits Ma had saved for guests.

qa.q: Why might Arnab have snapped 'You always tattle!' at Kalyani?
qa.a: After an hour of hard sums he seemed worn out and short of patience, so a small comment felt like too much.

qa.q: What might help Arnab after a long stretch of hard homework next time?
qa.a: A short break to play or eat a proper snack before anything else, like the cricket that settled him, could protect his patience.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Ma's explanation that his brain is tired?
qa.a: Kalyani isn't sure it's the whole reason and thinks he might also be fed up with sums, so the cause isn't certain.

grounding: An older sister watches her brother grab snacks and pick a fight after an hour of hard sums, unsure exactly why.

passage:
Monday: Parveen finished her easy spelling homework in ten minutes, then played ludo with her cousin Ujjwal without a single argument.
Wednesday: She spent an hour on a hard maths worksheet, frowning, erasing holes in the page. When she finished, she went straight for the chocolate tin she wasn't supposed to open before dinner. When Ujjwal moved a ludo piece, she snapped, "You're cheating!" and threw the dice under the sofa.
Friday: Another hard worksheet. This time, after forty minutes, Ammi said, "Stop. Ten minutes outside, then a banana, then finish." Parveen came back pink from running. She finished the last sums, ate her banana, and played ludo with Ujjwal. She lost, and just laughed.

qa.q: What did Parveen do right after the hard worksheet on Wednesday?
qa.a: She went straight for the chocolate tin she wasn't supposed to open before dinner.

qa.q: Why might Parveen have accused Ujjwal of cheating on Wednesday?
qa.a: After an hour of hard, frustrating work her patience seemed used up, so a small ludo move felt unfair.

qa.q: What choice did Ammi make on Friday, and how did it help?
qa.a: She broke up the hard work with ten minutes outside and a banana, and Parveen came back calmer, able to lose at ludo and laugh.

qa.q: What is it like for Ujjwal to play ludo with Parveen on Wednesday versus Friday?
qa.a: On Wednesday Ujjwal is blamed and the dice end up under the sofa; on Friday Ujjwal gets a cheerful cousin who laughs at losing.

grounding: Across a week, a girl grows impatient and grabs sweets after long hard sums, and a break changes how she copes.

passage: Gargi, you're grumpy after maths tuition, I can see it. Come, sit with your Neelam dadi. When I was ten, our master-ji made us do sums on slates for a full hour before recess. Long division, no talking. By the time the bell rang, I was a different girl. I'd grab my friend Sheela's roasted chana without asking and snap at anyone who touched my slate. My mother used to say, "The oil in your head's lamp has run out." Now your chacha, who reads about these things, tells me scientists argue over whether it's like oil at all. Maybe it was hunger, maybe boredom, maybe tiredness. I don't know. But I know this: after recess and a bit of running, I was sweet again. So go, play for twenty minutes. Then we'll talk.

qa.q: What did young Neelam grab from Sheela after the long division?
qa.a: Sheela's roasted chana, without asking.

qa.q: Why did young Neelam snap at anyone who touched her slate?
qa.a: After a full hour of silent sums her patience seemed worn thin, so small things irritated her.

qa.q: What does Neelam dadi suggest Gargi do after tuition, and why might it help?
qa.a: Play for twenty minutes first; a break and some running seemed to restore her own patience as a child.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel hearing that Neelam dadi was grumpy too?
qa.a: Gargi may feel understood rather than scolded, and more willing to take the break before talking 🙂.

grounding: A grandmother recalls losing patience after an hour of hard sums, noting that why it happens is still debated.

passage: The power went out at six, so Sarita did her fraction sums by the emergency lamp, sweating, for a full hour. She got the last one right on her fourth try. Then she went straight to the tin of namkeen Mummy kept for guests and ate handful after handful. When her cousin Himani sat in the only spot near the window, Sarita shouted, "That's MY place!" and yanked the cushion away. Himani's lip wobbled and she stared at the floor. Nani called Sarita over and felt her damp forehead. "All that thinking in this heat. Maybe you're worn out, maybe hungry, maybe just fed up. Hard to say which." Sarita flopped against her. "My head feels empty," she mumbled. "And I was mean."

qa.q: What light did Sarita use for her fraction sums?
qa.a: She did her fraction sums by the emergency lamp.

qa.q: Why did the namkeen tin feel impossible for Sarita to resist after her sums?
qa.a: After an hour of hard sums in the heat her head 'feels empty', so a treat feels like a fair reward and the rule about guests barely matters to her in that moment.

qa.q: What small step could help Sarita the next time a long, hard homework session ends?
qa.a: She could take a short break with water and an allowed snack before joining others, and say 'I'm tired' out loud instead of snapping at whoever is nearby.

qa.q: What is the evening like for Himani?
qa.a: For Himani the shout and the pulled cushion come out of nowhere, since she only sat by the window; she is likely hurt and confused about why her cousin turned on her 😢

grounding: A child who worked at hard sums for an hour raids the snacks and snaps at a cousin, while Nani treats the cause as uncertain.

passage: In their flat in Pune, Pooja spent an hour on the Olympiad practice paper, chewing her pencil and trying the tricky pattern question again and again. When she finally shut the book, her older sister Vasudha was eating biscuits on the sofa. Pooja grabbed three, then two more, though Aai had said none before dinner. When Vasudha changed the channel, Pooja snatched the remote. "You ALWAYS pick!" Vasudha raised her eyebrows. "You're cranky because of the maths. Your brain's out of fuel, I read it somewhere." Aai, chopping onions, said, "People argue about that fuel idea. Maybe she's tired, maybe bored and hungry. Either way, Pooja, drink some water and come help me." Pooja went, still sulking, and slowly her shoulders came down.

qa.q: How many biscuits did Pooja grab in all?
qa.a: She grabbed three, then two more.

qa.q: What might Pooja be feeling when she snatches the remote?
qa.a: She is worn out and irritable after an hour of hard questions, so a small thing like the channel feels deeply unfair and snatching seems justified to her.

qa.q: What choice did Aai make, and how did it help?
qa.a: Aai didn't argue about the cause; she gave Pooja water and a simple job in the kitchen, and Pooja calmed down as her shoulders came down.

qa.q: How does Vasudha's view of the grumpiness differ from Aai's?
qa.a: Vasudha is sure it is an empty fuel tank, while Aai treats the reason as uncertain and just offers something practical to help.

grounding: A child who spent an hour on hard maths grabs extra biscuits and snatches the remote, and the fuel-tank explanation is questioned.

passage: Last Sunday I did long division for one whole hour. Twenty sums, and they kept going wrong at the last step. When I finally finished, my head felt like cotton wool. I went to the kitchen and ate the whole packet of biscuits Mummy was saving for guests. Then my brother Pradeep asked to borrow my pencil, and I shouted at him to go away, which wasn't fair, because it was his pencil. Mummy found me sulking on the balcony. She said, 'Vinita, after a big hard job, brains often get cranky and hungry. Grown-up scientists still argue about exactly why. But it happens.' I said sorry to Pradeep. Now, after hard homework, I go on the swing for ten minutes before anything else.

qa.q: How many sums did Vinita do?
qa.a: Vinita did twenty sums.

qa.q: Why did Vinita shout at Pradeep over a pencil?
qa.a: Vinita felt tired and cranky after an hour of difficult sums, which left less patience than usual.

qa.q: What new habit did Vinita start, and why might it help?
qa.a: Going on the swing for ten minutes after hard homework gives a rest before dealing with snacks or people.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel being shouted at over his own pencil?
qa.a: Pradeep would likely feel confused and a bit hurt, since he only asked to borrow it.

grounding: A child remembers finding it harder to resist biscuits and keep her temper after an hour of hard sums, while the reason is still debated.

passage:
Tuition centre note, Thursday.
Today Mahima did a full hour of fraction practice for Saturday's test, the longest she has managed. She worked hard, frowning, and got most of them right. Straight after, the change was clear: she ate three packets of chips from the snack shelf in five minutes, then argued with Nakul about whose turn it was on the computer and pushed his chair. This isn't like her. I think after that much effort her patience simply ran low. Researchers still debate why this happens, and it may not be a simple 'running out' of willpower. Whatever the reason, the pattern was obvious today. I spoke with her calmly, she apologised to Nakul, and I told her mother at pickup. Plan: break the hour into two halves with a ten-minute outdoor break, and move snacks to before the session.
Harsha

qa.q: How many packets of chips did Mahima eat?
qa.a: She ate three packets in five minutes.

qa.q: Why did Mahima push Nakul's chair?
qa.a: After an hour of hard fractions she felt tired and her patience ran low, so a small disagreement felt much bigger.

qa.q: What changes does the tutor plan?
qa.a: Splitting the hour into two halves with a ten-minute outdoor break, and moving snacks to before the session.

qa.q: How might Nakul feel when Mahima pushes his chair?
qa.a: Nakul would likely feel surprised and upset, since this isn't how Mahima usually behaves.

grounding: A tutor's note shows a child losing patience and self-control after an hour of hard maths, while noting the cause is debated.

passage:
Friday
I did the algebra worksheet for a whole hour tonight, the hard one with brackets. By the end my brain felt fizzy and empty at the same time. Then I ate four of Abbu's chocolates, even though I'd promised to save them. Then Yash called to ask about the science project and I snapped at him for calling during dinner, which wasn't even true; it was after dinner.
I felt bad. I texted him sorry.
Abbu said that when brains work hard for a long time, people often get snappy and snacky. He said scientists argue about the exact reason, so nobody knows for sure, but he always feels it after long meetings too.
Tomorrow I'm going to do the worksheet before lunch, when I'm fresh, and nowhere near the chocolate tin.
Zeenat

qa.q: What kind of algebra worksheet did Zeenat do?
qa.a: Zeenat did the hard one with brackets.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat snap at Yash?
qa.a: After an hour of hard algebra Zeenat felt drained and short-tempered, so there was little patience left for Yash's call.

qa.q: What plan did Zeenat make for tomorrow?
qa.a: Doing the worksheet before lunch while fresh, and away from the chocolate tin.

qa.q: How might Yash feel being snapped at and then getting an apology?
qa.a: Yash might feel hurt at first but relieved to get the sorry text.

grounding: A child's diary shows snacking and snapping after an hour of hard algebra, with a parent noting the cause is not settled.

passage:
In the village school at Rampur, the teacher gave Alka a sheet of long-division sums for the whole last hour. Hard ones. She worked through them all, tongue out, rubbing out, trying again.
When the bell rang, she walked home along the canal with her brother Farhan, feeling wrung out.
At home, Ammi had kept a tin of laddoos for the evening guests. “Don't touch these,” she said.
Alka touched them. She ate two, then a third.
When Farhan said, “You'll get caught,” she snapped, “Mind your own business!” and shoved him.
Later, after roti and a nap on the charpai, she felt awful. “Sorry, Farhan,” she mumbled. “I was so tired from those sums. I just couldn't stop myself.”
Farhan shrugged. “You were really grumpy.”

qa.q: How long did Alka work on the long-division sums?
qa.a: She worked on them for the whole last hour.

qa.q: Why did Alka eat the laddoos and snap at Farhan?
qa.a: She felt drained and irritable after the hard sums, and her patience seemed to have run low.

qa.q: What could help Alka after a hard effort like that?
qa.a: A snack, a rest or a short walk before temptations and chores, so tiredness doesn't turn into grabbing or fights.

qa.q: How did Farhan experience Alka's mood?
qa.a: Farhan got shoved and saw her as grumpy, but he seems to accept her apology.

grounding: The passage shows a child who worked at hard sums for an hour finding it harder to resist snacks and picking a fight.

passage:
Jana had spent an hour at the kitchen table in Brno on her maths competition practice: fractions, then tricky word problems. When she finally closed the book, her head felt heavy.
Her little brother Bilal was eating crisps on the sofa. Usually Jana would have ignored him. Today she grabbed the bag. “Give me some.”
“Mum said no crisps before dinner!”
“You're eating them!”
They argued. Jana ate half the bag. When Bilal tried to take it back, she pushed his hand away hard.
Their mother came in. “What's going on?”
“I don't know,” Jana said, surprised at herself. “I'm just… tired. My brain's done.”
Mum looked at the maths book. “Hard session?”
Jana nodded. Mum handed her a glass of water. “Go outside for ten minutes. Then dinner.”

qa.q: What was Bilal eating on the sofa?
qa.a: He was eating crisps on the sofa.

qa.q: How did Jana feel after closing the maths book, and how did it show?
qa.a: She felt tired and irritable, which showed when she grabbed the crisps and pushed Bilal's hand.

qa.q: What did Mum suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Going outside for ten minutes, a break that may restore some patience before dinner.

qa.q: How might Bilal see his sister's behaviour?
qa.a: Bilal probably feels annoyed and confused, since she usually ignores his snacks.

grounding: The passage shows a child tired from an hour of hard maths finding it harder to resist snacks and picking a fight.

passage:
The olympiad training camp at the school ran from two to three: a full hour of geometry proofs. Jasleen, eleven, pushed through every one, even when her eyes blurred.
At three, the canteen opened. Jasleen had promised her mother no fried snacks this week. She bought two samosas.
In the corridor, Siddharth accidentally bumped her bag. “Watch where you're going!” she shouted. A few children turned.
Siddharth stared. “It was an accident.”
Jasleen sat on the steps and put her head in her hands. She knew she'd been rude. She also felt too tired to be sorry properly.
The camp teacher sat beside her. “Heavy hour, hmm? Brains get tired after proofs. Let's sit for five minutes.” After a while, Jasleen looked up and said, “Sorry, Siddharth.”

qa.q: How long was the geometry session?
qa.a: It was a full hour, from two to three.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen shout at Siddharth over a small bump?
qa.a: After an hour of hard proofs she felt exhausted and short-tempered, with little patience left.

qa.q: What did the camp teacher do that helped?
qa.a: The teacher named the tiredness without scolding and suggested a five-minute rest, after which Jasleen could apologise.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel being shouted at for an accident?
qa.a: Siddharth probably felt surprised and hurt, since he hadn't meant to bump her bag.

grounding: The passage shows a child tired after an hour of hard proofs giving in to snacks and snapping at a classmate.

passage:
Before: On the first day of the Pongal holidays, Leela helped her Paati draw kolam in the morning and shared murukku with her little sister Yamini without a fuss.
During: Two days later, Appa set her twenty word problems for the maths test after the break. Leela sat at the dining table for an hour, erasing and rewriting. When she finally closed the book, she marched to the kitchen, grabbed three murukku from the tin Amma had said to keep for guests, and ate them standing. Yamini asked for one. "Go away!" Leela shouted, and pushed her.
After: The next day, Amma broke the sums into four short sets with a walk between them. Leela finished without a fight. Amma wasn't sure if it was the breaks, the walk, or just that the sums got easier. Leela just knew her head felt less crowded.

passage:
"Harsha, you snapped at your cousin after tuition. Shall I tell you what your Ganga Paati did at your age?
It was the summer holidays, very hot, the year the well nearly dried. My father made me do long division every afternoon for one full hour. Big numbers, no fan. I would get it wrong, cross it out, start again.
After that hour, I was a different girl. I stole jaggery from the kitchen jar though Amma had forbidden it. I fought my brother over the swing. One day I tore his kite, just like that.
My father said my patience got used up, like oil in a lamp. These days, beta, I hear people argue whether it really works like that. Maybe I was just hot and hungry and fed up. But I know one thing. After that hour, I was not myself."

qa.q: What did Ganga do to her brother's kite?
qa.a: She tore his kite one day, just like that.

qa.q: How did young Ganga feel after the long hour of division?
qa.a: She felt worn out and irritable, "not myself", so resisting the jaggery or being kind to her brother became much harder.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have made those afternoons easier for young Ganga?
qa.a: Her father could have split the hour into shorter bits with a drink of water or a break, instead of one long hot stretch.

qa.q: What was it like for Ganga's brother on those afternoons?
qa.a: He probably felt hurt and confused, losing the swing and his kite to a sister who was fine earlier in the day.

grounding: It shows, through an elder's memory, a child who became less patient and more quarrelsome after an hour of hard sums, while noting the explanation is debated.

passage:
Holi week in the colony was loud: drums from the gate, children shrieking, water balloons thudding on the balconies. Mohit had an olympiad practice paper due the next morning, so he sat in the back room with the door shut and worked through the geometry problems for an hour, ears ringing.
When he came out, the plate of gujiya on the table was meant for the neighbours. He ate two, then a third, not really tasting them. His younger brother Vikas ran in, soaked in green. "Come play!"
"Don't drip on me!" Mohit shouted, much louder than he meant. Vikas's face fell.
Mummy looked from one to the other. "Is it the paper, or the noise, or the sugar?" she asked, half to herself. Nobody knew. Mohit went to the balcony and sat very still.

qa.q: How long did Mohit work on the geometry problems?
qa.a: He worked through them for an hour.

qa.q: What does Mohit's shouting at Vikas suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels drained and short-tempered after an hour of hard thinking in the noise, so a small splash sets him off.

qa.q: What small step could help Mohit next time he has a long practice paper?
qa.a: He could take short breaks between problems and have a planned snack ready, so he is less likely to grab sweets or snap afterwards.

qa.q: How does Vikas feel when Mohit shouts?
qa.a: Vikas feels hurt and deflated; he only wanted to share the Holi fun and did not expect his brother to bark at him.

grounding: It shows a child who worked hard on problems for an hour eating sweets he should not and snapping at his brother, with the cause left uncertain.

passage:
It was the week before Durga Puja, and the pandal music from the next lane came through the window while Nirmala sat at the table doing long division. One hour. Twenty sums. Her pencil had been sharpened four times.
When she finally shut the book, she went straight to the kitchen and ate three of the nimki Ma had kept for guests. Then Bidisha, her little sister, asked to borrow the red crayon, and Nirmala shouted, "No! Get your own!" and slammed the bedroom door.
Ma found her on the bed ten minutes later, face in the pillow. "Tired?"
"My head's full," Nirmala mumbled.
Ma sat down. "Long sums make everyone a bit short-tempered. Next time, a break halfway, and a snack that's allowed." Nirmala peeked out and nodded.

qa.q: How many sums did Nirmala do in the hour?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: Why did Nirmala snap at Bidisha over a crayon?
qa.a: After an hour of hard sums Nirmala felt worn out and irritable, her "head full", so small things felt like too much and her patience was gone.

qa.q: What could help Nirmala next time?
qa.a: As Ma says, a break halfway and an allowed snack; spacing out hard work may help her stay patient, whatever the exact reason tiredness makes it harder.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel when the door slams?
qa.a: Bidisha, who only asked for a crayon, probably feels startled and hurt, not knowing the shout was more about the sums than about her.

grounding: A child who worked hard at sums for an hour then grabs forbidden snacks and picks a fight, as mental tiredness seems to wear down her patience.
